facts.statement: A quarry worker named Xu Chengfa discovered the first fossil of Zhejiangopterus in April 1986 near the village of Aolicun in Linhai.
facts.quote: In April 1986 a young chalkstone quarry worker named Xu Chengfa found a large fossil near the village of Aolicun in Linhai.

facts.statement: The discoverer Xu Chengfa found three additional specimens before dying in an accident in 1988, while another worker later found a complete skull.
facts.quote: Xu himself managed to find three more specimens before being killed in an accident in 1988; another worker found a complete skull.

facts.statement: By the early 1990s, six large fossils had been recovered from the 81.5 million-year-old Tangshang Formation.
facts.quote: In the early 1990s, in total, six larger fossils had been recovered from the Tangshang Formation, an 81.5 million year old layer from the Campanian.

facts.statement: Paratypes include ZMNH M1325 (a skullless skeleton), ZMNH M1328 (an almost complete skeleton), and ZMNH M1329 (a fragmentary skeleton).
facts.quote: Several paratypes were referred: ZMNH M1325, a skeleton lacking the skull; ZMNH M1328, an almost complete skeleton and ZMNH M1329, a fragmentary skeleton.

facts.statement: The genus was named in 1994 by Chinese paleontologists Cai Zhengquan and Wei Feng.
facts.quote: The genus was named in 1994 by Chinese paleontologists Cai Zhengquan and Wei Feng.

facts.statement: The genus name refers to Zhejiang Province and the Latinized Greek word for 'wing'.
facts.quote: The genus name refers to the Zhejiang Province and a Latinized Greek pteron, "wing".

facts.statement: Zhejiangopterus lived in China during the late Cretaceous Period.
facts.quote: Zhejiangopterus is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur known from one species, which lived in China during the late Cretaceous Period.

facts.statement: Zhejiangopterus lived between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Zhejiangopterus was a moderately large pterosaur.
facts.quote: Zhejiangopterus was a moderately large pterosaur.

facts.statement: Initial wingspan estimates were 5 meters, later reduced to about 3.5 meters, with a body mass estimated at 7.9 kilograms.
facts.quote: Its wingspan was first estimated at 5 meters (16.4 feet). Later estimates reduced this to about 3.5 meters (11.5 ft), while its body mass is estimated by pterosaur expert Mark Witton to be around 7.9 kilograms (roughly 17 pounds) based on a volumetric method.

facts.statement: The skull was long, low, and perfectly arched, lacking a keel or crest.
facts.quote: Its skull was long, low, perfectly arched, and lacked a "keel" or any other crest sometimes seen in related species.

facts.statement: The nasal opening and antorbital fenestra merged into a single oval opening occupying nearly half the skull's length.
facts.quote: The nasal opening and the large opening typically present between the nose and eye openings of archosaurs (the "antorbital fenestra") had joined together in species such as this to create a single oval opening that occupied nearly one half the length of the skull.

facts.statement: The first six dorsal vertebrae fused into a notarium.
facts.quote: The first six dorsal vertebrae had fused into a notarium.

facts.statement: The femur was thin and long, measuring 1.5 times the length of the humerus.
facts.quote: Its femur was thin and long, 1.5 times longer than robust humerus.

facts.statement: Original describers classified Zhejiangopterus in Nyctosauridae due to its resemblance to the toothless Nyctosaurus.
facts.quote: Zhejiangopterus was classified as a member of the Nyctosauridae by the original describers because of the two edentulous pterosaurs they possessed good descriptions of, Pteranodon and Nyctosaurus, Zhejiangopterus more resembled the latter.

facts.statement: In 1997, David Unwin reclassified Zhejiangopterus into Azhdarchidae based on its relationship to Quetzalcoatlus.
facts.quote: In 1997 David Unwin determined that Zhejiangopterus was more closely related to this giant American form and thus belonged to Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: It was not until 1997 that David Unwin determined Zhejiangopterus belonged to Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: No fue hasta 1997 que David Unwin determinó que Zhejiangopterus estaba más cercanamente relacionado con este gigantesco género norteamericano y que por lo tanto pertenecía a Azhdarchidae.

facts.statement: To date, no other azhdarchid is known from such complete skeletal material.
facts.quote: Hasta la fecha no se conoce ningún otro azdárquido con un material del esqueleto tan completo.

facts.statement: Zhejiangopterus is classified in the family Azhdarchidae.
facts.quote: familia: Azhdarchidae

facts.statement: The genus authority is Cai & Feng, 1994.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Cai & Feng, 1994

facts.statement: The type species is Zhejiangopterus linhaiensis, described by Cai & Feng in 1994.
facts.quote: subdivision: Zhejiangopterus linhaiensis Cai & Feng, 1994 (especie tipo)

facts.statement: A cladogram placing Zhejiangopterus within Neoazhdarchia was recovered by Brian Andres and Timothy Myers in 2013.
facts.quote: The cladogram is based on a topology recovered by Brian Andres and Timothy Myers in 2013.
